newsitem.title: JAPAN: Philippines mulls tax break for finance firms.
newsitem.headline: Philippines mulls tax break for finance firms.

text.p: The Philippines may introduce tax exemptions for financial firms this year, central bank Governor Gabriel Singson told Reuters Financial Television on Friday.
Singson said the exemptions may be announced this year, but did not specify when they might take effect.
He said the Philippines was considering measures to designate some parts of the country as financial centres.
He said in order to do this "it is most important that we have to change our tax laws... We may even go to the extent of giving tax exemptions."
Asked when these measures might be announced, he said: "It's possible within this year."

But he added that the Philippines did not yet know if it was willing to pay the price of becoming a financial centre, saying the price was tax exemptions and the granting of absolute secrecy for bank deposit and corporate records.
Asked about the peso-dollar exchange rate in 1997, Singson said: "I expect the rate to be stable."
He also said he did not expect the yen's depreciation to accelerate.
"We don't expect the yen-dollar to depreciate as fast as it did in the last few weeks," he said.
He also said he did not expect rises in oil prices and wages to affect the inflation outlook of six to seven percent for 1997.

He said the central bank had studied the possible effects and concluded that an increase of one peso in fuel prices would result in an increase in inflation of 0.1 to 0.2 percent and that a wage increase of 20 pesos would only add about 0.1 percent. "We are very confident that it will still be at least for 1997 within that range," he said.
Asked about the effect of the weaker yen on the Philippine economy, Singson said the yen's depreciation helped the Philippines to service its debt.

He said one-third of the country's external debt and one-third of its reserves were yen-denominated but the reserves only amounted to 11.8 billion dollars while the total debt amounted 37 billion to 38 billion dollars.
"So, in a way the country benefits when the yen depreciates because in terms of U.S. dollars our debt becomes lower," he said.

Singson, on the last day of a three-day visit to Japan to promote foreign investment, added that he did not think the weaker yen would act as an disincentive for Japanese investors looking to the Philippines.
"I don't think that would be a big disincentive for them to come to the Philippines, unless the Japanese investors expect the yen to depreciate substantially," he said.
Singson said he believed Moody's Investors Service would upgrade the Philippines' sovereign debt this year.
"We are very confident that this will happen this year," he said.
He said a Japanese credit rating agency had already upgraded its assessment and that other agencies might also do so this year.
Moody's said on January 24 that it had placed the Philippines' foreign currency sovereign ceiling for bonds and notes under review for possible upgrade from the current Ba2 rating.
